paper_title: Entangle: Scaling Human-Video In-Context World-Action Models across Unseen Tasks and Contexts

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: In-context learning (ICL) enables foundation models to perform unseen tasks from context without parameter updates. In robotic manipulation, a human video provides the context that specifies how a task should be performed. However, scaling human-video ICL on world-action models (WAMs) faces two challenges: task-level human-robot pairs are not temporally aligned with robot actions, and standard action losses allow policies to rely on initial-scene or task-identity shortcuts rather than tracking the context. We present Entangle, an in-context world-action model that maps a single human video and current robot observations to future visual states and executable actions. To scale temporally aligned training data, we convert recorded robot videos into matched human contexts via video-to-video generation, supplemented by real paired recordings. For model training, we combine variable-length video windows with an intra-task contrastive objective that distinguishes the paired action trajectory from other executions of the same task, preventing task-identity shortcuts. Without task-specific fine-tuning, Entangle improves steadily as aligned training data scales, reaching an average score of 83.5/100 across six unseen tasks on an Astribot S1 robot, and achieves a 69.5% average success rate on seven unseen RoboTwin tasks, outperforming Zero-WAM by 22.6 percentage points. Under Context-OOD, although trained only on scene-aligned pairs, Entangle transfers context-specified behaviors across rearranged layouts and substituted tools. sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: In-context learning (ICL) enables foundation models to perform unseen tasks from context without updating model parameters [1]. In robotic manipulation, language instructions often underspecify multi-step order, spatial constraints, and fine-grained motion, whereas single human demonstration video directly shows how task should be performed [26]. World-action models (WAMs) [711], which jointly model future visual dynamics and robot control within shared generative backbone, offer natural foundation for such video-conditioned policies: given single human demonstration video as context, WAM can predict future visual states and executable actions for unseen manipulation tasks without parameter updates. However, scaling human-video ICL on WAMs faces two core challenges. First, human and robot videos are typically paired only at the task level. Whether collected independently or synthesized from an edited initial frame via text-to-video generation [9, 12], task-level pairs share high-level goal but diverge in motion paths, contact timing, and execution speed. Without temporal alignment between the human video and ground-truth robot actions, the model cannot localize which segment of the demonstration corresponds to target action chunk, reducing the video prompt to coarse task label. Second, even when paired trajectories are aligned, standard action-prediction losses supervise each trajectory in isolation and leave room for shortcuts: when task admits multiple valid executions (e.g., different manipulation orders or obstacle-avoidance paths), policy can lower its loss by inferring the task identity or relying on the initial scene layout rather than tracking the specific progression shown in the demonstration. To address these challenges, we present Entangle, an in-context world-action model that maps single human demonstration video and current robot observations to future visual states and executable actions. First, to scale temporally aligned training data, we convert recorded robot videos into matched human demonstrations via reference-conditioned video-to-video (V2V) generation, supplemented by real paired recordings  (Fig. 2)  . Unlike first-frame editing followed by text-driven generation, V2V translation preserves the camera viewpoint, object interactions, and timing of the source robot trajectory, so each generated human video remains temporally aligned with the recorded ground-truth actions. Second, we encode the human demonstration and current robot observations in shared video-action backbone and concatenate their tokens along the temporal axis  (Fig. 3)  . For model training, we combine variable-length video windows with an intra-task InfoNCE contrastive objective [13] inspired by negative-aware fine-tuning [14]: by pulling predicted actions toward the video-paired trajectory while repelling other trajectories of the same task, it prevents task-identity shortcuts and forces the policy to follow the demonstrated motion. We evaluate Entangle on an Astribot S1 robot and the RoboTwin benchmark [15, 16]. Without task-specific fine-tuning, Entangle improves steadily as aligned training data scales, reaching an average score of 83.5/100 across six unseen tasks on Astribot S1, and achieves 69.5% average success rate on seven unseen RoboTwin tasks, outperforming Zero-WAM [9] by 22.6 percentage points. More surprisingly, although our training pairs are strictly scene-aligned, Entangle goes beyond unseen tasks with the same objects (Fig. 1, middle): it transfers the demonstrated behavior across rearranged layouts and substituted tools, such as using banana to sweep wooden block into cardboard box from brush-and-dustpan demonstration (Fig. 1, top and bottom). Our main contributions are as follows: Scalable temporally aligned data: we turn recorded robot trajectories into temporally matched human demonstrations with reference-conditioned video-to-video generation, so alignment scales with the robotvideo corpus without human reenactment. In-context WAM training: we concatenate demonstration and robot-video tokens along time, train on variable-length windows, and add an intra-task InfoNCE loss that removes the task-identity shortcut. Data scaling and cross-scene transfer: unseen-task scores grow monotonically with aligned data; scenealigned training transfers to new layouts and tools.

sections.title: 2.1 In-Context Learning for Robotic Manipulation
sections.content: In-context learning enables frozen robot policy to infer task from deployment demonstrations, such as sensorimotor trajectories in ICRT [3], demonstration graphs in Instant Policy [4], or retrieved segments in RICL [5], extending one-shot policies based on task embeddings [17, 18], frame attention [19, 20], or skill priors [2123]. To leverage human videos, prior works learn visual features [24], latent actions [25], or play plans [26], co-train on egocentric data in EgoMimic [27], retrieve play segments in RHyME [28] and MimicDroid [29], or condition deployment on single human video via video retrieval in ViP [30], language grounding in BC-Z [31], and cross-attention in Vid2Robot [2]. However, reducing demonstration to task identifier limits policies to recalling training behaviors [32], whereas generalizing to unseen procedures and novel object uses requires tracking how the interaction unfolds, as explored through subgoal or trace prediction [3335], temporal alignment [3639], intra-task keyframe separation in JEDI [40], layout shifts in SimpleICL [41], and functional substitutions in The Imitator Game [42]. Entangle uses single human video to specify the procedure within world-action model, generalizing across unseen procedures (Task-OOD) and altered scenes or tools (Context-OOD).

sections.title: 2.2 World-Action Models
sections.content: World-action models jointly predict future observations and actions [10, 4346], extending visual foresight [47], action recovery from visual plans [4850], predictive representations for control [5153], and video generators adapted for policy learning [7, 11, 5456] or rollout synthesis [57]. Recent WAMs further incorporate context and demonstrations: ICWM [58] infers system properties from self-interaction, WATCH [59] pretrains on task-paired human videos, LingBot-VA 2.0 [8] and WorldScape Policy 2.0 [60] accept demonstration prompts, and Zero-WAM [9] generates task-matched human clips while predicting temporally spaced future chunks to encourage prompt usage. However, conditioning on demonstration alone does not ensure that predicted actions follow the demonstrated execution over task-level cues; Entangle addresses this by combining temporally aligned training with intra-task action contrast [13] to distinguish different executions of the same task.

sections.title: 2.3 Test-Time Training
sections.content: Meta-imitation adapts policy parameters from demonstration [61, 62], while test-time training adapts models or fast weights to test inputs [6365]. WAM-TTT [66] updates fast weights from human videos before rollout, and RoboTTT [67] updates them as the robots visuomotor history grows. Entangle keeps its weights fixed at deployment, conditioning each prediction directly on the human demonstration and current robot observation.

sections.title: 2.4 Motion Retargeting and Paired Data
sections.content: Motion retargeting transfers object-relative motions [68, 69] or human hand trajectories [7072] to robot; BEHAVE [73] records humanobject contact, and CORE4D [74] retargets two-person rearrangement motions to new object shapes. Robot training data can also come from paired humanrobot recordings [7577] or synthesizing robot demonstrations from human footage [7881], whereas Gen2Act [82] generates human video from an initial image and task description. Entangle uses the full robot recording as motion reference, verifies the generated human video for temporal and interaction agreement with the source, and combines these clips with synchronized human reenactments so each sampled demonstration window pairs directly with the recorded robot actions.

sections.title: 3.1 Dataset Overview and Strict Pairing
sections.content: Each training example in the Ent-Dataset pairs human demonstration video with recorded robot trajectory containing camera observations, proprioceptive states, and actions (Fig. 2(c)). As summarized in Fig. 2(b), the dataset contains 21.3k pairs split across disjoint robot episodes for training and validation, comprising 5.3k real pairs from Astribot S1 (Ent-Real) and 16.0k synthetic pairs from Astribot and AgiBot (Ent-Syn). 3 Figure 2 Overview of the Ent-Dataset. (a) Ent-Syn pipeline: source robot trajectories undergo (1) keyframe hand editing, (2) motion-guided video generation, and (3) VLM verification for visual quality and action consistency, before pairing the generated human video with the original robot observations and actions. (b) Dataset composition: concentric rings (from inner to outer) break down all 21,269 paired episodes by data source (Ent-Real, Astribot, AgiBot), human-video source (Human, Seedance, Wan), train/validation split (19,115 / 2,154), and task category (635 tasks). (c) Paired demonstrations: examples from the Ent-Real and Ent-Syn subsets across five matched timestamps, illustrating temporally aligned robot and human executions. To supervise fine-grained action prediction from human video, each target action chunk requires localized visual reference in the demonstration. When human and robot videos are paired only by task label or synthesized from an edited initial frame [9], subsequent motion paths and contact timing remain unaligned with the ground-truth robot actions. To provide unambiguous supervision, we enforce strict pairing: using the recorded robot trajectory as an anchor, the paired human video matches (i) the camera viewpoint and scene layout, (ii) the manipulated objects and sequence of interaction events (e.g., reaching, grasping, transporting, and releasing), and (iii) the timing of each event. This alignment requires the policy to track visual progression instead of relying on initial-scene or task-identity shortcuts; we ablate strict pairing in Table 2 and evaluate cross-scene transfer at deployment in Section 5.6.

sections.title: 3.2 Ent-Real
sections.content: We construct real pairs by having humans reenact recorded Astribot S1 trajectories in the same workspace under viewpoint matched to the robots head camera. During recording, demonstrators watch the source robot video playback and perform the manipulation in synchrony, matching the object interactions, motion paths, and execution tempo.

sections.title: 3.3 Ent-Syn
sections.content: To scale the paired corpus without per-episode human reenactment, we convert existing robot videos into human demonstrations through three-stage pipeline (Fig. 2(a)). Keyframe editing. We extract atomic action descriptions from the robot-video annotations (including Qwen3.84 generated descriptions) and sample source keyframes for appearance editing. Using human-hand images from HaGRID [83] as appearance references, gpt-image-2 replaces visible robot arms and grippers with human hands and forearms while preserving the scene, task objects, viewpoint, and contact relationships. The edited frames pass visual quality checks before video generation. Video generation. Using Seedance 2.5 or Wan 3.0, the video editor takes the complete source robot clip as motion reference, the edited keyframes as appearance references, and text prompt with the atomic action description. Supplying the full robot clip anchors action timing, object trajectories, and state transitions throughout generation without requiring explicit segmentation masks, depth maps, or edge-map control. Verification and pairing. visionlanguage model (VLM) verifier filters generated clips for visual quality (complete arm replacement and scene stability) and temporal action consistency with the source trajectory; verified clips are paired with the original robot observations and actions (details in Appendix E.4).

sections.content: We first formulate human-video-conditioned in-context manipulation, then present the Entangle architecture and its training recipe combining an intra-task InfoNCE contrastive objective with variable-length window training.

sections.title: 4.2 Model Architecture
sections.content: Figure 3(a) illustrates the Entangle architecture. The human demonstration ctx and the robot video (It, ) are encoded by the shared 3D VAE into spatiotemporal latent grids of Fc and Fq frames, respectively, where the demonstration latents and current observation It remain clean (σv = 0) while future robot latents σv are noised. The patchified video tokens form unified stream HV , processed alongside the projected action tokens HA. Mixture-of-Transformers with directional attention. Following Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) design [9, 10, 46], our WorldAction DiT backbone keeps modality-specific QKV projections, normalization layers, and feed-forward networks for the video and action streams, and couples the two only through shared attention. As in the base model, early blocks run the streams independently; in the remaining blocks, action queries attend to video keys, whereas video queries never attend to action keys (Fig. 3(a)). This asymmetry 5 lets the action stream read context-conditioned visual features without noisy action tokens perturbing video generation. Temporal RoPE alignment. Video tokens use 3D rotary positional embeddings (RoPE) over temporal, height, and width coordinates (t, h, w), alongside additive camera-view embeddings; action tokens use 1D temporal RoPE. The three layouts in Fig. 3(b) differ only in which axis is reset or offset per segment: temporal reset shares the spatial grid (h, w) but assigns both segments identical t; spatial offset makes (h, w) disjoint but breaks cross-segment correspondence; our temporal offset makes disjoint while sharing (h, w). This layout assigns the human context (t {0, . . . , Fc 1}) and robot video (t {Fc, . . . , Fc + Fq 1}) sequentially along the time axis, preserving spatial correspondence without temporal collision. Correspondingly, action temporal positions are anchored to the start of the robot video segment instead of = 0 (Fig. 3(b)): πA(k) = Fc + ρ , (3) where is the action step index and ρ is the action-to-latent temporal ratio. Dynamically shifting πA(k) by Fc keeps action tokens temporally aligned with the robot video segment across variable context lengths. Figure 3 Overview of Entangle. (a) Human context and the current robot observation condition joint videoaction prediction, with action tokens attending to video tokens. (b) Temporal RoPE places context and robot video sequentially while preserving local spatial coordinates, and anchors action positions to the robot segment. (c) Each inference round jointly denoises future video and actions, executes an action prefix, and replans with updated observations and context.

sections.title: 4.3 Training
sections.content: We initialize from MotuBrain [10] and continue training (CT) on the full Ent-Dataset (Sec. 3) with the objectives below. We evaluate CT directly on the real robot; RoboTwin uses multi-task supervised fine-tuning (SFT) for simulator adaptation. Intra-task InfoNCE contrastive objective. The flow-matching loss LWAM (Eq. 2) supervises each trajectory in isolation: when task admits multiple valid executions (e.g., different visiting orders or obstacle-avoidance paths), it does not explicitly penalize predictions that drift toward other valid trajectories of the same task, allowing the policy to rely on coarse task identity inferred from It without tracking ctx. Inspired by negative-aware fine-tuning [14], we introduce an intra-task InfoNCE objective [13] that contrasts the one-step 6 θ,i (from noised action input Xi = clean-action estimate bAi = Xi σiua σi,i at noise level σi) against other trajectories of the same task in the batch. Let Gi denote same-task samples in the batch (Gi 2) and d( bAi, Aj) the mean squared distance between bAi and clean trajectory Aj. We pull bAi toward its context-paired trajectory Ai while repelling same-task alternatives {Aj}jGi{i} so task identity alone provides no shortcut: LInfoNCE = 1 X iB log exp[d( bAi, Ai)/τ ] jGi exp[d( bAi, Aj)/τ ] , (4) where τ is temperature and the set of valid anchors, giving the total loss = LWAM + λInfoNCELInfoNCE. Variable-length window training. Context window duration governs trade-off between procedural following and generalization: conditioning on full-episode clips encourages the model to infer global task identity and complete the task semantically instead of following the context, whereas training only on short clips limits temporal context and hurts generalization. To balance this trade-off, we randomly sample synchronized human and robot windows across multiple durations (13, 25, or 37 frames, encoding to Fc {4, 7, 10} latent frames) with the matching action segment; the anchored RoPE in Eq. 3 keeps actions aligned at every window length. Closed-loop inference with Adaptive Horizon (AH). When executing predicted action chunk open-loop, later steps can lose grounding in the human reference as future uncertainty grows, accumulating contact and trajectory errors before the next observation. In each replanning round (Fig. 3(c)), we therefore monitor attention from predicted actions to the reference tokens: when later steps exhibit low reference-attention weight and high temporal entropy (indicating weak, diffuse grounding in the demonstration), Adaptive Horizon (AH) truncates execution to the reliable prefix (624 steps), advances the context window by the executed duration, and replans from fresh observations. sections.title: 5 Experiments
sections.content: We evaluate Entangle on the RoboTwin benchmark [15, 16] and physical Astribot S1 robot across two generalization axes: Task-OOD, where the complete goal and multi-step procedure are absent from training data, and Context-OOD, where the execution scene departs from strictly aligned training pairs through rearranged layouts or substituted objects and tools.

sections.title: 5.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Inference protocol. Both simulation and real-robot inference condition purely on 13-frame human-video window without language input, using 50 denoising steps and video/action guidance scales of 5 and 1. Simulation (RoboTwin). We address the simulator domain shift with joint SFT on 43 RoboTwin training tasks, then evaluate on seven unseen tasks. Context advances 13 frames per prediction round. Real robot 7 (Astribot S1). We evaluate the CT model directly without downstream SFT, predicting 24 action steps at 10 Hz (2.4 s) and executing 624 steps per round via AH (or all 24 steps without AH; Appendix E.3). Metrics. We report binary success rates in simulation and graded task scores (0100) on the real robot. Real-robot scores are averaged over 10 trials per task and configuration, measuring completion of both the demonstrated goal and procedural constraints (rubrics in Appendix A.3).

sections.title: 5.2 RoboTwin Benchmark Evaluation
sections.content: We evaluate seven RoboTwin tasks excluded from SFT training under the Zero-WAM demo_clean protocol [9]: three seeds and 100 episodes per task per seed, with one fixed generated human context per task. Entangle reaches 69.52%, exceeding Zero-WAM (46.95%) by 22.57 percentage points  (Table 1)  and the agent-based RoboICL (32.38%) by 37.14 points. While Zero-WAM competes well on single-object tasks (e.g., opening microwave, placing cup), it scores 9.00% on three-block stacking (SB), versus Entangles 70.33%. This gap indicates that task-matched clips generated from an edited initial frame suffice for short, single-stage actions, whereas frame-aligned correspondence is critical for multi-step sequences.

sections.title: 5.3 Real-Robot Task-OOD Evaluation
sections.content: The six Astribot S1 tasks are absent from pretraining and CT. They test block manipulation (object roles and ordering), mouse use (novel grasping, surface motion, and clicks), towel wringing (bimanual coordination), counterintuitive goals (unconventional destinations), sweeping (using cup as tool), and obstacle avoidance (following specified passage beyond reaching the goal; Fig. 4). Appendix gives task definitions, and Appendix pairs human contexts with robot executions. Figure 4 Six real-robot tasks with execution frames in chronological order. The cyan arrow in (f) marks the required left opening. Component controls. Table 2 ablates strict pairing, same-task trajectory contrast (InfoNCE), variable-length training (VL), and adaptive horizon (AH); the full model leads on five of six tasks (83.5 mean). Replacing reference with another same-task episode at training time (w/o pairing, 41.3) conveys coarse intent on Blocks, but collapses fine bimanual twisting (Towel), trajectory tracking (Mouse), and counterintuitive placement: task-level pairing cannot supervise fine motion or counter-prior goals. Without InfoNCE (64.7), the policy drifts toward an average path that collides with the obstacle, degrading multi-route tasks (Avoidance and Mouse). Fixed 13-frame training (w/o VL, 62.7) restricts the model to myopic local mappings that fail to connect the detour passage to the goal, reducing Avoidance to zero. Finally, executing all 24 steps open-loop (w/o AH, 61.3) hurts Avoidance and Towel, as executing later steps after reference attention weakens accumulates route and contact errors. Thus, data-level alignment, training-level contrast, and deployment-level replanning are all essential.

sections.title: 5.5 Data Scaling on Real-Robot Task-OOD
sections.content: We evaluate five nested CT-data fractions (0%, 10%, 25%, 50%, and 100%) on the six real-robot tasks  (Fig. 5)  , where 0% evaluates the pretrained backbone directly and nonzero fractions train for 4,000 CT steps. Without aligned CT data (0%), the pretrained backbone scores zero across all tasks; as aligned data scales from 10% to 100%, the mean score rises monotonically from 40.8 to 83.5. Across tasks, small fraction (10%25%) already suffices to ground highlevel intent such as object ordering (Blocks), counterintuitive destinations (Counterintuitive), and tool repurposing (Sweeping), whereas continuous bimanual coordination (Towel) and strict route adherence (Avoidance) require 50%100% of the corpus. This indicates that while modest paired data teaches the policy what object or goal to target, scaling temporally aligned data via our synthetic pipeline is essential for translating how human moves into fine-grained robot control. sections.title: 5.6 Context-OOD Evaluation
sections.content: Because all training pairs are strictly scene-aligned, we evaluate four progressively harder Context-OOD shifts  (Fig. 6)  to examine how Entangle establishes correspondence when the workspace departs from the reference. Under spatial layout shift (reoriented pens) and within-category substitution (black to white mouse), the policy adapts its grasp orientation and reproduces the same letter-tracing trajectories across mouse appearances. Under affordance-preserving cross-object transfer and affordance repurposing, the policy transfers interactions across object categories, adapting hold-and-wipe from picture frame to stand and using banana to sweep wooden block into box when brush and dustpan are absent. Thus, supervising strict temporal alignment on world-action prior does not lock the policy into pixel-level copying; instead, Entangle exhibits an emergent ability to transfer demonstrated interactions to novel objects and scenes, freeing deployment from strict scene alignment to accommodate diverse demonstrations.

sections.title: 5.7.1 With and Without InfoNCE
sections.content: Cloth rotation and toss. Both policies receive the same reference, in which the human lifts cloth, moves it in circle, and tosses it toward the picture frame. With InfoNCE, the wrist rotation more closely matches 9 Figure 6 Four types of Context-OOD, shown as compact process sequences. (c) Picture-frame-to-stand transfer preserves the hold-and-wipe interaction. (d) banana takes the unconventional role of sweeping tool. the demonstration. The robot opens its gripper but fails to toss the cloth. Without InfoNCE, the robot only partially follows the demonstrated circular motion but successfully tosses the cloth  (Fig. 7)  . Figure 7 Cloth rotation and toss in two rollouts conditioned on the same human video. Schematic arrows show circular or side-to-side motion during the turning phase and the toss or drop direction in the final column. The cloth color differs across the rollouts. Wiping the back of picture frame. Both policies receive the same reference, in which the human flips the frame, steadies it with the left hand while wiping with the right, and withdraws both hands. With InfoNCE, the left gripper holds the frame throughout wiping. The robot then retracts its arms as shown in the context video. During retraction, the frame gets snagged on one of the grippers. Without InfoNCE, the left gripper withdraws early and the right wipes near the edge without the demonstrated support  (Fig. 8)  . Intra-task InfoNCE favors the trajectory paired with the current video among alternatives for the same task. In these examples, the policy trained with InfoNCE follows the demonstrated procedure more closely. The runs without it show both the flexibility and the cost of taking alternative trajectories. different wrist motion produces successful toss, while the early withdrawal during wiping omits the demonstrated support.

sections.title: 5.7.2 Deployment with Generated Video Context
sections.content: We condition Astribot S1 on Seedance-generated video. The video shows the left hand pushing the pen holder forward and the right hand gathering three pens beside it. The robot successfully follows the two-step procedure zero-shot  (Fig. 9)  . This example illustrates how video generation model can serve as zero-shot visual planner [12, 82]. sections.title: 5.7.3 Execution Without Task Objects
sections.content: The human picks up pen with the right hand, passes it to the left hand, and places it in holder. On an empty tabletop, the robot closes its right gripper, brings both grippers together, and opens the right gripper while the left remains closed. It then opens the left gripper at the end of the placement motion, preserving the order and hand roles of the demonstration  (Fig. 10)  . Figure 10 The robot reproduces the demonstrated handover motions on an empty tabletop. With the pen and holder absent, the scene provides no object-state cues for the transfer. The preserved handover sequence and release order demonstrate the policys ability to follow the context video.

sections.title: 6 Limitations and Future Work
sections.content: Our real-robot evaluation is limited to one embodiment, and the data pipeline relies on the fidelity of generated human videos. Cross-scene transfer and generated-context deployment are demonstrated through qualitative cases; broader quantitative evaluation is needed. Future work will explore cross-embodiment transfer, more reliable data generation, and failure recovery for longer tasks.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented Entangle, which uses human video as an interface for specifying robot behavior without taskspecific parameter updates. Our findings suggest that learning from aligned humanrobot experience can support transferable demonstration following beyond familiar tasks and scenes. This offers path toward more accessible robot adaptation, where people can communicate new behaviors by showing how they should be performed.

sections.content: A Real-Robot Tasks, Environments, and Scoring A.1 Capability Coverage and Task Selection We checked the MotuBrain pretraining and continued training (CT) data for the goal and full procedure of each evaluation task. OS: Object on scale (place_object_scale). mouse, stapler, or bell and an electronic scale are placed on the same side of the table. E.4 Paired Dataset Construction and Split Checks Episode-level split. target robot episode can be paired with multiple human videos. We assign all pairs that share target episode to the same split and verify that training and validation share no target episode identifiers. Synchronous human reenactment. Participants first practice following the source robot video, then record while watching its playback and synchronizing the manipulation with it. They use viewpoint matched to the head camera and mimic the grippers grasping and release motions with their hands while avoiding dexterous finger manipulations that the parallel gripper cannot reproduce. All human demonstrations record only tabletop hand and forearm manipulations without faces or personally identifiable information, and were collected with participant consent. Keyframe editing and video generation. Source robot-video annotations, including Qwen3.8-generated descriptions, provide the atomic action condition. Selected source frames are edited with gpt-image-2 using HaGRID human-hand appearance references. The edit preserves the source scene, objects, viewpoint, and contact relationships while replacing robot manipulators with human hands and forearms. Edited frames are quality-checked before serving as appearance references for video editing with Seedance 2.5 or Wan 3.0. The complete source robot clip provides the motion reference, together with the action description and scene-preservation instructions. No explicit robot-arm segmentation mask, depth map, or edge map is supplied to the generator. Accepted human clips retain the original robot observations and actions as supervision. Cross-embodiment action supervision. Both Astribot and AgiBot recordings supply paired videoaction training examples. AgiBot examples retain their own recorded actions under the shared action representation, with dimension-validity masks identifying available action components. They contribute video and action supervision during CT; real-robot deployment is evaluated on Astribot S1. VLM screening. We sample frames at the midpoints of equal-duration intervals within each clip and present them to visionlanguage model (VLM) in chronological order. For paired comparisons, the source and generated frames occupy two rows, with each column matching the same relative time in the two clips. The visual-quality check tests for complete replacement of visible robot manipulators, absence of residual robot geometry, anatomical hand and forearm appearance, scene stability, and motion continuity. Task tools already present in the source are distinguished from robot residue. Skin-colored rigid robot links or gripper shapes fail the check even when their surface appearance resembles skin. For the source-alignment check, the verifier receives the paired frames and the source action description. It checks action identity, left/right roles, timing of the main phases, trajectories, object states, and absence of additional manipulation. Different hand poses, incidental contact after placement, and small differences in release or withdrawal timing are allowed when the main manipulation and resulting object states agree. Changing the target object, reversing transport direction, or continuing to manipulate an object after the source action ends fails this check. The verifier returns pass/fail decision for each check. We retain generated clip only if it passes both.
